name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (ACME CFI-G)
hardware: ACME spherical porous burner modules with cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes and thermocouples
sample: Spherical porous burner, inverse and normal diffusion flames
objective: Determine the conditions in which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane and n-pentane, in normal and inverse flames, over a broad range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature and fluent flow rate, supported by CFD and kinetics.
approach: Spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the ISS with multiple fuels, reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions.
varied: fuel, O2 mole fraction, pressure, fluent flow rate, flame direction (normal or inverse)

findings.text: The CFI-G experimental table in PSI holds 154 tests with usable O2 and pressure, spanning 12 to 85 percent O2 and 7.2 to 48.0 psia, for ethane, propane and butane inverse flames.

In CFI-G, spherical gas-fueled cool diffusion flames were obtained only for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar and an ambient O2 mole fraction of 0.39; they were not readily produced elsewhere in the matrix. Burner temperature was found to matter.

habitatRelevance: Foundational: cool flames emit little heat and light and may escape optical detection; the PSI table covers up to 85 percent O2 but not the 34 percent, 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere as a labelled point.

name: ACME Flame Design
objective: Study the production and control of soot to optimise oxygen-enriched combustion and design robust soot-free flames.
habitatRelevance: Oxygen-enriched flames and radiative extinction behaviour are relevant to elevated-O2 habitats.

name: ACME Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
sample: Coflow laminar diffusion flames, fuel diluted with N2
objective: Extend the range of flame conditions accurately predicted by validating kinetic and soot sub-models at extremes of fuel dilution, from sooty pure fuel to near-extinction dilute flames.
habitatRelevance: Benchmark data for combustion models; no habitat-atmosphere conditions reported.

name: ACME Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
hardware: Burner with mesh electrode, up to 10 kV
sample: Coflow laminar diffusion flames in electric fields
objective: Understand flame ion production and how electric fields control non-premixed flames, including stability, soot and emissions.
varied: applied electric field, with and without air coflow
habitatRelevance: Ion wind acts as a controllable weak flow on a buoyancy-free flame; no habitat-atmosphere conditions reported.

name: ACME Structure and Response of Spherical Flames
sample: Spherical diffusion flames, soot-free and sooty
objective: Predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and pulsating instabilities, of soot-free and sooty spherical diffusion flames.
habitatRelevance: Radiative versus convective extinction limits inform model validation; no habitat conditions reported.

name: Structure and Liftoff in Combustion Experiment
objective: Obtain coflow diffusion flame data from near-extinction to heavily sooting conditions to study gravity effects on flame liftoff, blowout and soot formation.
habitatRelevance: Soot and blowout behaviour in microgravity; no habitat conditions reported.

name: Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment
sample: Coflow laminar diffusion flames at the smoke point
objective: Measure laminar smoke points of coflow diffusion flames in microgravity against normal gravity.

findings.text: SPICE: the smoke-point flame length in microgravity increases with coflow velocity and decreases with burner diameter, correlating as d^-0.77 times u^0.48 (burner diameter d, coflow velocity u) in one analysis and d^-0.67 times u^0.27 in another.
SPICE sooting propensity ranking in the thesis analysis: methane is lowest, then ethane, ethylene, propane and propylene highest.

habitatRelevance: Sooting propensity data relevant to smoke production; no habitat conditions reported.

name: OpenFOAM cool flame CFD using FLEX data
objective: CFD of cool flames validated against ISS FLEX droplet data (title as given in the PSI listing; page not available).

findings.text: FLEX discovered cool flames: after a large heptane droplet's visible flame dies by radiative extinction, the droplet keeps vaporizing, sustained by soot-free low-temperature chemistry. A visibly dead fire can still be releasing fuel vapour.

name: Flamelet-generated-manifold concurrent flame spread compared with BASS
objective: Flamelet-generated-manifold modelling of solid-fuel flame spread compared with BASS data (title as given in the PSI listing; page not available).

findings.text: The flammability boundary is U-shaped in O2 against flow speed. The low-flow branch is quenching by radiative loss, observed near about 1 cm/s for thin fuels, and is unreachable in 1 g where buoyant flow is at least about 20 cm/s.

name: SPICE soot analysis
objective: Soot analysis reusing SPICE data (title as given in the PSI listing; page not available).

name: Cool flame counterflow extinction using FLEX
objective: Counterflow cool-flame extinction compared with FLEX data (title as given in the PSI listing; page not available).

findings.text: FLEX discovered cool flames: after a large heptane droplet's visible flame dies by radiative extinction, the droplet keeps vaporizing, sustained by soot-free low-temperature chemistry. A visibly dead fire can still be releasing fuel vapour.

name: SAME smoke simulation
objective: Smoke transport simulation using Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment data (title as given in the PSI listing; page not available).

findings.text: Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in low gravity is sub-micron: a substantial fraction of particles is below 500 nm in SAME, and most average sizes are 200 to 400 nm in SAME-2, with larger particles in some quiescent cases. Smoke transport is dominated by mixing, so detection lags are longer than in 1 g.

name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)
hardware: Porous circular gas burners, 25 and 50 mm
objective: Establish burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties, using CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 on 25 and 50 mm porous burners in O2/N2 ambients at the planned atmospheres of 14.7 psia and 21 percent, 10.2 psia and 26.5 percent, and 8.2 psia and 34 percent O2, plus O2/CO2 and extinction limits.
approach: Establish chamber diluent, O2 and pressure, start fuel flow and ignite, then observe quasi-steady burning until extinction, burner temperature equilibrium or heat-flux sensor limit; later reduce fuel flow stepwise to find the extinction limit.
varied: ambient O2, pressure, burner size, fuel flow

findings.text: BRE microgravity flames emulating condensed fuels burned quasi-steadily in elevated-oxygen atmospheres without any airflow, whereas such flames in a normal 21 percent O2 atmosphere self-extinguished in a short time. The atmospheres planned for the flights were 14.7 psia and 21 percent, 10.2 psia and 26.5 percent, and 8.2 psia and 34 percent O2.

In BRE, flames self-extinguished within 40 s at 21 percent O2 but burned steadily at 26.5, 34 and 40 percent O2 (ethylene/N2 burner of 25 and 50 mm, 0.57 to 1 bar). 34 percent is the 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere.

habitatRelevance: Planned flights include the 8.2 psia, 34 percent O2 atmosphere; flames self-extinguished at 21 percent but burned steadily in elevated-O2 atmospheres.

name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)
hardware: Small wind tunnel in the glovebox, airflow up to 40 cm/s
sample: Rods, spherical sections, slabs, films and fabric sheets
objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity and begin bridging NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground microgravity tests and real microgravity flammability.
approach: Fuel samples in a small wind tunnel in the MSG with crew support; oxygen varied below 21 percent by adding nitrogen; opposed and concurrent flow.
varied: flow speed and direction, O2 concentration, sample geometry

findings.text: BASS-II reports that PMMA rods sustain spread at 17 percent O2 in microgravity against 18 percent in 1 g, and that microgravity spread was faster at all comparable O2 levels and diameters. The test matrix spans 0.4 to 8 cm/s and 15 to 21 percent O2 in opposed flow.
findings.value: 17 percent (0 g) vs 18 percent (1 g) O2

findings.text: The flammability boundary is U-shaped in O2 against flow speed. The low-flow branch is quenching by radiative loss, observed near about 1 cm/s for thin fuels, and is unreachable in 1 g where buoyant flow is at least about 20 cm/s.

habitatRelevance: Reduced-O2 flammability limits; tests Test 1 assumptions but no lunar-pressure or elevated-O2 data.

name: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
hardware: Small flow duct, 76 mm by 76 mm cross section, airflow up to 40 cm/s
sample: Fabrics, spheres and cylinders, with igniter wire
objective: Bridge the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground microgravity tests and real microgravity flammability, including wake flames, and assess an inert gaseous extinguishing agent over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow.
approach: Samples in a flow duct in the MSG ignited with a Kanthal wire; fan airflow in opposed or concurrent direction; flame size, shape, colour, spread rate and quenching recorded.
varied: flow direction and speed, material, geometry, suppressant

findings.text: The 1 g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 limits are not conservative: materials burn in microgravity at lower O2, by up to 4 percent O2 mole fraction. Mylar G has a 1 g upper limiting oxygen index of 20.8 percent against 17 percent in 0 g at 10.2 psia.
findings.value: up to 4 percent O2 lower in 0 g

findings.text: Spread depends on duct confinement: smaller microgravity tunnels gave faster spread than Saffire because hot gas accelerates in the confined duct. A fire behind a panel may therefore be more hazardous than one in open cabin volume.

habitatRelevance: Direct test of Test 1 conservatism and nitrogen suppression in microgravity; ambient conditions not stated on the PSI page.

name: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
objective: Examine combustion of n-dodecane and its mixtures at pressures of 0.25 to 5 atm, analyse helium dilution effects on cool flames, and relate droplet size, pressure and extinction, including soot formation during cool-flame combustion.
approach: Droplets dispensed in the MDCA chamber with a hot-wire igniter; gas mixtures diluted with oxygen, nitrogen and helium; black-and-white, UV (OH*) and high-resolution cameras plus radiometers.
varied: pressure, He dilution, fuel mixture, droplet size

findings.text: CFI studies cool-flame burning of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures and farnesane droplets at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm, including the effect of helium dilution on cool-flame behaviour and soot formation during cool-flame combustion.

FLEX discovered cool flames: after a large heptane droplet's visible flame dies by radiative extinction, the droplet keeps vaporizing, sustained by soot-free low-temperature chemistry. A visibly dead fire can still be releasing fuel vapour.

habitatRelevance: Cool flames may persist after a hot flame extinguishes; chamber O2 values are not stated on the PSI page.

name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / DAFT-2
hardware: Modified TSI P-Trak particle counter with DustTrak control, Mylar aerosol bags
objective: Mitigate the risk for SAME by demonstrating that a modified TSI P-Trak counts aerosol correctly in microgravity, comparing it with the DustTrak, and creating aerosol standards.
approach: Modified P-Trak using capillary action to recycle isopropanol; Arizona Red Dust aerosolized with GN2 and measured on orbit against the DustTrak.
habitatRelevance: Instrument feasibility for smoke detection; no combustion conditions.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment-2 (FLEX-2)
sample: Free or fiber-supported droplets, single and binary arrays
objective: Extend FLEX to fuels and conditions that mimic real combustors and provide benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion, including flame extinction boundaries, soot formation and droplet interactions.
approach: Chamber filled to 0.5 to 3.0 atm with O2 mole fraction 0.1 to 0.4 and diluent gas balance; droplet deployed, ignited and tracked with high-speed and colour video.
varied: fuel, ambient gas composition, pressure, droplet diameter, droplet velocity, droplet spacing
habitatRelevance: Extinction boundaries across 10 to 40 percent O2 and 0.5 to 3 atm; diluent species not stated on the page.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
objective: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure the effectiveness of CO2, He and SF6 suppressants, and develop predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity.
approach: Determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as a function of pressure (0.5 to 1.5 atm) and suppressant by repeating droplet tests at progressively lower ambient O2 until droplets fail to ignite.
varied: pressure, O2 mole fraction, suppressant and concentration, droplet size

findings.text: FLEX measured the limiting oxygen index (LOI) of droplets: methanol burns down to about 12 to 13 percent O2 in O2 and inert-gas mixtures (0.7 and 1 atm, 12 to 30 percent O2, CO2 or He 0 to 70 percent).

Reported FLEX LOIs (O2 mole fraction): O2/N2 about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for heptane; with CO2 about 0.14 and 0.17; with He at 1 atm about 0.14 and 0.15. CO2 raises the heptane LOI by about 2 points, whereas He barely changes it.

FLEX discovered cool flames: after a large heptane droplet's visible flame dies by radiative extinction, the droplet keeps vaporizing, sustained by soot-free low-temperature chemistry. A visibly dead fire can still be releasing fuel vapour.

habitatRelevance: Gives inert-diluent suppressant effectiveness; LOI at the 8.2 psia exploration pressure is not reported.

name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
platform: Cygnus resupply vehicle after ISS departure
hardware: Saffire flight unit with sample card in a large flow duct
sample: Fabric 0.94 m long by 0.4 m wide
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and investigate low-g flammability limits compared with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.
approach: Large SIBAL sample ignited in a duct with fans at 20 cm/s; cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, O2 and CO2 sensors and anemometers; data compressed and downlinked.

findings.text: In the large Saffire fabric burns in microgravity, concurrent-flow flame spread over the SIBAL fabric (40.6 by 94 cm, in air at about 21.5 percent O2 and 1 atm) reached a steady rate of 1.8 mm/s in Saffire-I (20 cm/s duct flow) and 2.3 mm/s in Saffire-III (25 cm/s). In 1 g the same sample burns completely and the fire accelerates.
Opposed-flow (upwind) spread in microgravity was sustained at 1.3 mm/s in Saffire-I and 0.98 mm/s in Saffire-III, whereas the 1 g downward-burn analogue did not propagate.
Saffire flames reached a steady flame length: about 40 mm for concurrent spread and about 24 mm for opposed spread, rather than growing without limit as the 1 g fire does.
findings.value: about 40 mm concurrent; about 24 mm opposed

findings.text: Spread depends on duct confinement: smaller microgravity tunnels gave faster spread than Saffire because hot gas accelerates in the confined duct. A fire behind a panel may therefore be more hazardous than one in open cabin volume.

habitatRelevance: Largest-scale microgravity fabric fire; shows steady spread and flame length in air.

name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II)
platform: Cygnus resupply vehicle after ISS departure
hardware: Saffire flight unit, sample card of nine 5 by 29 cm samples
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and investigate low-g flammability limits compared with NASA's normal-gravity test.
approach: Sample card with nine samples in a flow duct at 20 or 30 cm/s, concurrent or opposed, depending on material; same instrumentation as Saffire-I.

findings.text: Saffire-II used small 5 by 29 cm samples at about 22.1 percent O2 with mixed results: silicone did not ignite in microgravity although it burned completely in 1 g, cotton-fiberglass burned completely, and Nomex burned about 5 cm in microgravity (about 0 in 1 g).
findings.value: SIBAL 2.1 mm/s at 20 cm/s; 2.6 mm/s at 25 cm/s

habitatRelevance: Multi-material flammability in microgravity at slightly elevated O2.

name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III)
platform: Cygnus resupply vehicle after ISS departure
hardware: Saffire flight unit with large flow duct
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and investigate low-g flammability limits compared with NASA's normal-gravity test.
approach: SIBAL sample as in Saffire-I but at a higher flow velocity, concurrent or opposed; cameras, thermocouples, radiometers and gas sensors.

findings.text: In the large Saffire fabric burns in microgravity, concurrent-flow flame spread over the SIBAL fabric (40.6 by 94 cm, in air at about 21.5 percent O2 and 1 atm) reached a steady rate of 1.8 mm/s in Saffire-I (20 cm/s duct flow) and 2.3 mm/s in Saffire-III (25 cm/s). In 1 g the same sample burns completely and the fire accelerates.
Opposed-flow (upwind) spread in microgravity was sustained at 1.3 mm/s in Saffire-I and 0.98 mm/s in Saffire-III, whereas the 1 g downward-burn analogue did not propagate.
Saffire flames reached a steady flame length: about 40 mm for concurrent spread and about 24 mm for opposed spread, rather than growing without limit as the 1 g fire does.
findings.value: about 40 mm concurrent; about 24 mm opposed

habitatRelevance: Shows flame spread rate and steady flame length at a higher flow; PSI page states 30 cm/s, the paper table 25 cm/s.

name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R)
hardware: SAME hardware with a new M-pass instrument
objective: Quantify the particle sizes that smoke achieves in low gravity and relate them to smoke generation and transport conditions.
approach: SAME hardware with Pyrell foam replacing DBP, higher heating temperatures and no-flow heating; 66 test points were flown July 16 to September 9, 2010.

findings.text: SAME-R flight tests ran from July 16 to September 9, 2010, completing 66 test points, with Pyrell intumescent foam replacing the DBP samples and new no-flow heating conditions.

Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in low gravity is sub-micron: a substantial fraction of particles is below 500 nm in SAME, and most average sizes are 200 to 400 nm in SAME-2, with larger particles in some quiescent cases. Smoke transport is dominated by mixing, so detection lags are longer than in 1 g.

habitatRelevance: Smoke size data for spacecraft detector design; ambient O2 and pressure not stated on the PSI page.

name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
hardware: Near-field hardware, far-field box, thermophoretic samplers and two smoke detectors
objective: Quantify the sizes liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and relate droplet size distribution to smoke generation and transport; develop a code to predict droplet growth.
approach: Crew installed hardware in the glovebox; igniter on for 15 to 60 s; thermophoretic soot samplers analysed after flight by TEM; detector response recorded from video.
varied: sample temperature, flow field, particle ageing time

findings.text: Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in low gravity is sub-micron: a substantial fraction of particles is below 500 nm in SAME, and most average sizes are 200 to 400 nm in SAME-2, with larger particles in some quiescent cases. Smoke transport is dominated by mixing, so detection lags are longer than in 1 g.

habitatRelevance: Smoke particle size baseline for detector design.
